item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: Out of curiosity: if this is an electromagnetic phenomenon, would the Foundation attempt shielding the effect with a Faraday cage? It seems like a logical step, and fairly easy to test. I'm honestly not familiar with how effective that type of shielding is at limiting broadcasts (typically used, as it is, to shield equipment from outside interference), but another option would be to employ electromagnetic waveguides and/or externally-generated magnetic fields to shape the effect into a more consistent and containable form. All of that is dependent on the field's source and frequency, though; some frequencies are easier to shape than others, and if the frequency's being modulated over a range then that could make it practically impossible to attenuate.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Can someone explain the necessity of surgically disabling subjects' vocal cords and training them in Morse code? That's the only detail giving me significant pause; it seems like a needless waste of effort when there is no specified reason (none that I saw, at least) that a subject could not outline his or her 'nightmares' verbally.

Otherwise, right now it feels sort of like you're skimming over the surface in a couple areas. Mostly generalizing the "deleterious effects" of exposure and secondhand descriptions of subject's dreams. This would draw me in a lot more if there was an audio log or something of one of the subjects dreaming. Or a little extra detail concerning the incidents that necessitated revisions to the object's containment procedures, with a choice [REDACTED] or two.

The latter would probably be a better path to attempt, since a log of any sort would take more effort to do well and be a more significant addition in an article that just needs a little something extra to top it off. In my opinion.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
In the story this skip comes from, the researcher goes through a checkout procedure where she says a test phrase into some machinery while having her vital signs monitored. It's part of a process designed to help staff confirm that they're in the real world and not at the beginning of some recurring nightmare sequence brought on by SCP-480, the prospect of which was unnerving staff.

I didn't put it in the article, but my notion was that staff members undergo a psychological conditioning regimen designed by the same office of neurology or whatever that's working on conditioning the test subjects. Staff are encouraged to think of the passphrase while also thinking about some action or memory that triggers an area of the brain less likely to be active during REM sleep, and that helps to develop a system to distinguish reality from dream.

"Memetic" may have been the wrong word (I know it's routinely abused around here). But I thought it fit, anyway.

item.content:encoded:
Being unable to reconcile "differences too subtle to be perceived" with the example used ruins this for me. Driving a highway doesn't leave much room for "subtle differences" that can go unnoticed. An alteration of one degree can get you honked at within seconds in the right traffic. And how many iterations would have to run to go from "didn't take the exit" to "took the exit"?

I'll just be picking up the pieces of my immersion then.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It's a recurring nightmare chamber, which is a cool enough idea. But the many-worlds bit seems forced and ruined it for me.

Addendum 1 gives no actual reason, it boils down to "because I said so, and we have to assume it's the most dangerous option." The thing is, having the visions be "real", for certain definitions of the term, doesn't make this thing more dangerous. An unknown party inducing nightmares for inscrutable SCIENCE! reasons is no less of a threat than the same party giving glimpses of actual quantum-reality deviations for SCIENCE!

Which is the other thing that bugged me, but not as much. Why do they assume there is a controlling intelligence? I see nothing to support that. The anomaly is "calmer" when it has a subject, but that could be a completly non-sapient reaction, something tied to the observer effect. To me, that would be better fridge logic.
